claims.statement: Catullus preserves the recoverable functional shape of the hanging line's three constraints — adversative turn, universalizing move, comparative-illustrative case — and *reverses the polarity of each element within its preserved functional form* (#1052 §6): endurance becomes destruction; low-case exemplification (the beggar, the poor person) becomes high-case exemplification (*reges et beatas urbes* — kings and blessed cities); preservation becomes ruination. statements.quote: Catullus preserves the recoverable functional shape of the hanging line's three constraints — adversative turn, universalizing move, comparative-illustrative case — and *reverses the polarity of each element within its preserved functional form* (#1052 §6): endurance becomes destruction; low-case exemplification (the beggar, the poor person) becomes high-case exemplification (*reges et beatas urbes* — kings and blessed cities); preservation becomes ruination. **Catullus.** Catullus 51 preserves the poem's shape into Latin and answers the hanging line at a distance, inverting each pole of its inscribed comparison — the low case becomes *reges … et beatas urbes*, endurance becomes destruction — and then ends there, on *perdidit urbes*, with no return to the erotic frame: a translation that terminates in its own suspension. And Catullus does more than fill the terminal socket; he occupies the initial one. He is the later man who sits face-to-face with the text and receives the voice across six centuries — **Catullus is κῆνος**, the seat of line 1 taken by the reader the deixis had reserved for him.¹⁷

claims.registered_title: Γλῶσσα Ἔαγε: The Tongue Breaks Twice — On the Two Ruptures in Sappho 31 and the Voice That Answers the Second
claims.statement:
**πᾶν τολματόν** is not a finite verb at all. It is a **verbal adjective in -τός**: *all [is] to-be-dared*. Neuter, predicative, and **incapable of taking a nominative doer.** The form names an action as available and leaves the agent slot structurally open. The rupture here is in the **agency** — and what fills it is the reader.

**The line says a daring and makes you dare.**

statements.quote: Its last transmitted form is τολματόν (P: παντόλματον, one word) — a verbal adjective in -τός, structurally incapable of governing a nominative agent: an act with no doer.² Between the two, the frame closes on its own verb — φαίνεταί μοι… φαίνομαι, *he appears to me* … *I appear* — and the second person of the poem, a voice and a laugh with no face, no body, no name, is best identified as the poem itself: the speaker's archived self, seen in the act of being read. What sets the heart flapping in the breast (τὸ… ἐπτόαισεν) is exact on this reading: the sight of her own transmission.³

claims.registered_title: The Socket and the Stamp: Sappho 31.17 as Completed Composition and Longinus 10.2–3 as the First Filling
claims.statement:
**And the address is bare.** The treatise's second-person perception verbs after quotations carry a vocative without exception:

```
ὁρᾷς        ὦ ἑταῖρε     addressed
ἐπιβλέπεις  ἑταῖρε       addressed
θαυμάζεις   ⟨ nothing ⟩  BARE
```

**θαυμάζεις is the one that names nobody.** A question posed to no addressee is posed to whoever is holding the text. **Longinus fills Sappho's socket with a socket of his own** — hers withholds the agent of an action, his withholds the answerer of a question — and the load passes straight through him to the reader.

**This is the propagation mechanism, and it is why the form does not exhaust.**
